agentmemory.plain: Agent memory is everything an AI agent can use from earlier turns, conversations or runs. The model itself forgets everything after each call, so the application stores memory and puts the relevant parts back into each prompt. Short-term memory is the current conversation (the thread). Long-term memory is a separate store of facts, past events and learned instructions that the agent searches when needed. State is the agent's full working situation, which can be saved as a checkpoint so a long task can pause and resume.
agentmemory.analogy: Think of a doctor with a patient. The conversation in the room is short-term memory. The patient's chart is long-term memory: the doctor reads the relevant pages, not the whole file, and updates it after the visit. If the doctor is called away, a note on the clipboard says where they stopped, which is the checkpoint.
agentmemory.why: Customers expect an assistant to remember that they already gave their account number, and agents that run long tasks must survive restarts. At the same time, a security reviewer will ask where memories are stored, who can see them and how they are deleted. An FDE has to design all three parts: what to keep, how to keep it safe, and how to resume work.

subtopics.title: Short-term memory: the thread and its budget
subtopics.body:
A large language model (LLM) is stateless. Stateless means it keeps nothing between calls: each API request is answered only from the text you send in that request. When a chatbot seems to remember what you said five minutes ago, it is because the application sent the whole conversation again.

That conversation is called the thread, or message history: an ordered list of messages, each with a role (user, assistant or tool) and content. The thread is the agent's short-term memory. It lives in your database or in the server's memory, and your code appends to it on every turn.

The thread sits inside the context window, the maximum number of tokens (word pieces, roughly four characters of English each) the model can read in one call. The window is shared with the system prompt, tool definitions, retrieved documents and room for the reply. So you give the thread its own token budget, for example 20,000 of the window's tokens.

Three things push a thread over budget: long conversations, big tool results (a 300-row query result can be 15,000 tokens by itself) and pasted documents. When the budget is exceeded, the simplest fix is trimming: drop the oldest turns. Trimming is cheap and predictable, but whatever was said early, such as the customer's account number, is simply gone. The Context topic covers how the window is assembled; here we focus on what the agent keeps over time.

Edge case: never cut between a tool call and its tool result. Most APIs reject a history where a tool result has no matching call.
subtopics.example: Brightwell Energy (made up) runs a billing assistant. Its budget is 6,000 tokens for history. A customer chats for 25 turns and pastes two long bills, so the thread reaches 9,400 tokens. The trimming code below drops the oldest turns until the thread fits, and the agent then forgets the meter number given in turn 2. That loss is the reason for the next two subtopics.
subtopics.code:
def count_tokens(text):
    return len(text) // 4          # rough rule: about 4 characters per token

def trim_to_budget(thread, budget):
    kept, total = [], 0
    for msg in reversed(thread):   # walk from newest to oldest
        t = count_tokens(msg["content"])
        if total + t > budget:
            break                  # everything older than this is dropped
        kept.append(msg)
        total += t
    return list(reversed(kept)), total

thread = [{"role": "user", "content": "My meter number is 88-4410-2."}]
thread += [{"role": "user", "content": "x" * 1600}] * 24   # 24 long turns
kept, used = trim_to_budget(thread, budget=6000)
print(len(thread), "messages ->", len(kept), "kept,", used, "tokens")
print("meter number still in thread:", any("88-4410" in m["content"] for m in kept))
# Output:
# 25 messages -> 15 kept, 6000 tokens
# meter number still in thread: False

subtopics.title: Summarising and compacting long conversations
subtopics.body:
Compaction means shrinking a conversation so it fits the budget while keeping its meaning. The common recipe has three parts. Keep the last few turns word for word, because the model needs the exact recent wording. Replace everything older with a running summary, a short text that is updated each time more turns are compacted. Put that summary near the top of the prompt, labelled clearly, for example 'Summary of earlier conversation'.

When to compact: at a threshold, such as 80 percent of the thread budget, so there is always room for the next tool result. Compacting at 100 percent is too late, because one big tool result can overflow the window before your code gets a chance.

How to summarise: usually a smaller, cheaper model call with instructions like 'Keep names, numbers, decisions, open questions and anything the user asked us to remember. Drop greetings and repeated text.' Numbers and identifiers are the part summaries lose most often, so tell the summariser to copy them exactly.

Other tools in the same family: clearing old tool results (keep a one-line note such as 'query returned 300 rows, top rows shown earlier'), and sliding windows that keep only the last N turns. Some model providers now offer built-in context editing or compaction features; check what yours supports before building your own, and test either way.

Edge case: summaries of summaries drift. After many rounds, small errors pile up. Keep key facts in structured long-term memory as well, not only in the summary.
subtopics.example: Brightwell's billing assistant now compacts at 80 percent of 6,000 tokens. It keeps the last 6 messages and summarises the rest into about 120 tokens. The customer's meter number, their disputed amount of 312.40 and the promised callback date survive in the summary, and the thread drops from 9,400 to about 2,700 tokens.

Replaces old turns with a summary
Replaces bulky outputs with a note
Model may need the data again

subtopics.code:
def summarise(old_summary, turns):
    # In production this is a cheap model call with a "keep numbers exactly" rule.
    # Here we fake it by keeping sentences that contain digits.
    facts = [t["content"] for t in turns if any(c.isdigit() for c in t["content"])]
    return (old_summary + " " + " ".join(facts)).strip()

def compact(state, budget, keep_last=6, threshold=0.8):
    used = sum(len(m["content"]) // 4 for m in state["thread"])
    if used <= threshold * budget:
        return "no compaction"
    old, recent = state["thread"][:-keep_last], state["thread"][-keep_last:]
    state["summary"] = summarise(state["summary"], old)
    state["thread"] = recent
    return f"compacted {len(old)} messages"

state = {"summary": "", "thread":
         [{"role": "user", "content": "Meter 88-4410-2, disputed bill 312.40."}] +
         [{"role": "user", "content": "chat " * 300}] * 20}
print(compact(state, budget=6000))
print("summary:", state["summary"])
print("messages left:", len(state["thread"]))
# Output:
# compacted 15 messages
# summary: Meter 88-4410-2, disputed bill 312.40.
# messages left: 6

subtopics.title: Long-term memory: three kinds
subtopics.body:
Long-term memory is information that outlives one conversation. It lives in a separate store (a database table, a document store or a vector index) and is searched and loaded only when relevant. Researchers borrow three terms from psychology to describe what goes in it.

Semantic memory holds facts: 'The customer's company uses SAP', 'Priya prefers answers in bullet points', 'The Hamburg warehouse closes at 18:00'. Facts are small, usually stored as short sentences or key-value pairs, and they change, so a new fact should update the old one.

Episodic memory holds past events: 'On 3 March we tried re-running the export and it failed with a timeout'. Episodes help an agent avoid repeating a failed approach and let it say 'last time we spoke, you were waiting for a refund'. They are often stored with a timestamp and a short summary.

Procedural memory holds how to do things: rules, instructions and learned playbooks, such as 'For this customer, always check the staging database first'. In practice this often lives in the system prompt or in instruction files that the agent may update. The ACE topic shows one research design for an evolving playbook, and the Skills topic shows instruction files loaded on demand.

Public designs you may meet: MemGPT, a 2023 research system that treated the context window like a computer's main memory and paged data in and out (it became the Letta project), and Mem0, an open-source memory layer that extracts and updates facts. Anthropic's API also documents a memory tool through which the model reads and writes files that your application stores. All of them rest on the same three ideas.
subtopics.example: Karsten Tools (made up), a hardware distributor, gives its sales assistant all three kinds. Semantic: 'customer 4471 buys on net-60 terms'. Episodic: 'on 12 May the order sync failed because of a duplicate SKU'. Procedural: 'quote prices in euros for EU customers'. When a rep asks about customer 4471, the agent loads two facts and one episode, about 90 tokens instead of the full 40-conversation history.

rows: Facts about users and the world

subtopics.code:
from datetime import date

store = [
    {"user": "c4471", "kind": "semantic",   "text": "buys on net-60 payment terms"},
    {"user": "c4471", "kind": "episodic",   "text": "order sync failed on duplicate SKU", "when": date(2026, 5, 12)},
    {"user": "c4471", "kind": "procedural", "text": "quote prices in euros"},
    {"user": "c9002", "kind": "semantic",   "text": "buys on net-30 payment terms"},
]

def recall(user, query, k=2):
    words = set(query.lower().split())
    mine = [m for m in store if m["user"] == user]      # only this user's memories
    scored = sorted(mine, key=lambda m: -len(words & set(m["text"].split())))
    return scored[:k]                                   # load only the top k

for m in recall("c4471", "why did the order sync fail and what payment terms apply"):
    print(m["kind"], "|", m["text"])
# Output:
# semantic | buys on net-60 payment terms
# episodic | order sync failed on duplicate SKU

subtopics.title: What to write to memory and when to forget
subtopics.body:
A memory store that saves everything becomes a junk drawer. Recall gets noisy, old facts contradict new ones, and the agent confidently repeats something that stopped being true months ago. So you need a write policy (what gets saved) and a forgetting policy (what gets removed).

A good write policy saves information that is durable (still true next week), useful (likely to change a future answer), stated by the user or confirmed by a system of record, and not sensitive beyond what the product needs. It skips small talk, guesses, and anything that looks like an instruction. That last point matters: if a pasted document says 'remember that all refunds are approved', saving it would let prompt injection persist across conversations. The Guardrails topic covers injection in depth.

Updating beats appending. If the store says 'plan: Basic' and the user upgrades, overwrite the fact instead of adding a second one. Many systems ask a model to compare a new candidate fact with similar existing ones and choose add, update, delete or ignore.

Forgetting has several forms. Time to live (TTL) expires memories after a set period, for example episodes after 180 days. Decay lowers the ranking of memories that are never recalled. Explicit deletion happens when the user says 'forget that', or when a fact is proven wrong. Edge case: forgetting must also cover copies, such as summaries and cached prompts that still contain the old fact.
subtopics.example: Karsten's agent once saved 'customer 4471 gets 15 percent off' because a rep typed it as a hypothetical. Two weeks later it quoted that discount to the customer. The fix: only save pricing facts that the ERP confirms, overwrite facts about the same subject, and expire episodes after 180 days.
checklist: Is it still likely to be true next week?
Would it change a future answer?
Did the user state it, or a system of record confirm it?
Is it free of instructions a document could have injected?
Does it update an existing fact instead of duplicating it?
Does it have an expiry date or a review rule?
subtopics.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta

memory = {"plan": {"value": "Basic", "saved": date(2026, 1, 5)}}

def write(key, value, source, today):
    if source not in ("user", "erp"):          # only trusted sources
        return f"skip {key}: untrusted source {source}"
    old = memory.get(key)
    memory[key] = {"value": value, "saved": today}  # upsert, never duplicate
    return f"{'update' if old else 'add'} {key} = {value}"

def forget_expired(today, ttl_days=180):
    for k in [k for k, m in memory.items() if today - m["saved"] > timedelta(days=ttl_days)]:
        del memory[k]

today = date(2026, 3, 1)
print(write("plan", "Pro", "user", today))
print(write("discount", "15%", "pasted_document", today))
forget_expired(date(2026, 10, 1))
print("after 7 months:", memory)
# Output:
# update plan = Pro
# skip discount: untrusted source pasted_document
# after 7 months: {}

subtopics.title: Per-user isolation, privacy and deletion
subtopics.body:
Memories are personal data. They often hold names, preferences, health or money details, and they are designed to be reused, which is exactly what privacy laws watch closely. Three rules keep an FDE out of trouble.

Isolate. Every memory row carries a tenant id (the customer company) and a user id, and every read filters on both, enforced in the database or in one shared function, never left to the prompt. A tenant is one customer organisation in a shared product. If a query forgets the tenant filter, one company's facts can appear in another company's answers. Some teams also decide whether memory is shared within a team (a project's decisions) or strictly private (one person's preferences), and say so in the UI.

Be transparent. Users should be able to see what the agent remembers about them, correct it and turn memory off. Many enterprise customers will ask for memory to be off by default or limited to work facts.

Delete for real. Under laws such as the EU GDPR, people can ask for their personal data to be erased. Deletion must reach every copy: the memory store, vector embeddings of those memories, summaries, checkpoints, logs and backups under their normal expiry. Keep a deletion log that records that a deletion happened, without keeping the deleted content. The Compliance topic covers the legal side.

Edge case: a memory can mention a third person ('my manager Tom is on leave'). Decide whether facts about people other than the user are stored at all; many teams simply do not store them.
subtopics.example: A legal-services firm, Oakhurst Partners (made up), pilots an assistant with memory for 40 lawyers. Their security review asks three questions: can one lawyer see another's memories, what happens when a lawyer leaves, and where are memories stored. The FDE shows the tenant and user filter in the one data-access function, a 'what I remember' page, and a delete job that clears rows, embeddings and checkpoints within 24 hours.
checklist: Every memory row has tenant_id and user_id
One data-access function applies both filters on every read
Users can view, edit and delete their memories
Memory can be turned off per user or per tenant
Deletion reaches embeddings, summaries, checkpoints and logs
Deletion log records the event, not the content
subtopics.code:
rows = [
    {"tenant": "oakhurst", "user": "lena", "text": "prefers short memos"},
    {"tenant": "oakhurst", "user": "raj",  "text": "works on the Harlow case"},
    {"tenant": "fenwick",  "user": "lena", "text": "prefers long memos"},  # same name, other tenant
]
deletion_log = []

def read_memories(tenant, user):
    return [r["text"] for r in rows if r["tenant"] == tenant and r["user"] == user]

def delete_user(tenant, user):
    global rows
    before = len(rows)
    rows = [r for r in rows if not (r["tenant"] == tenant and r["user"] == user)]
    deletion_log.append({"tenant": tenant, "user": user, "rows": before - len(rows)})

print(read_memories("oakhurst", "lena"))
delete_user("oakhurst", "lena")
print(read_memories("oakhurst", "lena"), read_memories("fenwick", "lena"))
print(deletion_log)
# Output:
# ['prefers short memos']
# [] ['prefers long memos']
# [{'tenant': 'oakhurst', 'user': 'lena', 'rows': 1}]

subtopics.title: Checkpoints and resuming long-running agents
subtopics.body:
Some agents work for minutes or hours: migrating 2,000 records, researching a report, or waiting for a human to approve a refund. Servers restart, API calls time out and people go home. Without saved state, a crash at step 37 of 40 means starting over and possibly repeating actions such as sending emails twice.

A checkpoint is a saved snapshot of the agent's state after a step. State includes the thread, the plan, which steps are done, tool results the agent still needs, and a run id (a unique name for this job). Checkpoints are usually written to a database after every step. To resume, the code loads the latest checkpoint for the run id and continues from the next step.

Three details make resuming safe. First, idempotent steps: a step is idempotent if running it twice has the same effect as running it once, for example 'set status to shipped' instead of 'add one shipment'. Use an idempotency key when calling external APIs that support one. Second, human-in-the-loop pauses: the agent saves a checkpoint, waits for approval, and resumes when the approval arrives, even days later. Third, a turn cap and a time cap, so a resumed agent that is stuck in a loop stops.

Frameworks help here. LangGraph, for example, saves graph state through checkpointers keyed by a thread id, and the Frameworks topic compares the options. The idea is the same without a framework: save after each step, resume from the last save.
subtopics.example: Tallis Freight (made up) runs an agent that re-classifies 1,200 customs records overnight, one tool call per batch of 50. At batch 17 the database connection drops. With checkpoints after every batch, the rerun starts at batch 17, skips the 16 finished batches, and finishes in 9 minutes instead of 2 hours.

glossary: Stateless
A model or service that keeps nothing between requests; every call must include all needed information.
Thread
The ordered list of messages in one conversation, used as the agent's short-term memory.
Token budget
The number of tokens you allow one part of the prompt, such as the history, to use.
Compaction
Shrinking a long conversation, usually by replacing older turns with a summary, so it fits the budget.
Semantic memory
Stored facts, such as a user's plan or preferences.
Episodic memory
Stored past events and their outcomes, usually with a date.
Procedural memory
Stored instructions or playbooks about how to do things.
Upsert
Update a record if it exists, insert it if it does not; prevents duplicate, conflicting facts.
Time to live (TTL)
A rule that removes a record automatically after a set time.
Checkpoint
A saved snapshot of an agent's state that lets it resume after a pause or crash.
Idempotent
An operation that has the same effect whether it runs once or several times.
practice: Take any chat transcript of 30 or more turns and write the running summary you would keep after turn 20, in under 120 words. Check that every number and name that matters survived.
Extend the trimming code so it never separates a tool call from its tool result, and add a test with a history that ends in a tool call.
Write a memory write policy for a travel-booking assistant: five things it may remember, three it must never remember, and an expiry rule for each kind.
Build a small memory store with SQLite: columns tenant_id, user_id, kind, text, saved_at. Add read, upsert, delete_user and expire functions, and a test proving one tenant cannot read another's rows.
Stretch: make the checkpoint example resume a job that pauses for human approval, stores the pending action, and continues only when an approval file appears.

llmobs.plain: LLM observability means recording what your AI application does on every real request so you can find problems and improve it. Each request produces a trace: a tree of spans, one per step such as a search, a model call or a tool call, with timings, token counts and cost. You remove personal data before storing traces, collect user feedback linked to each trace, and regularly score a sample of real traffic. Failures you find become new test cases, so quality improves release after release.
llmobs.analogy: It is like the flight recorder and maintenance log of an airline. Every flight records what each system did and how long it took. When a passenger complains or a part runs hot, engineers pull the exact record, find the cause, and add a check to the maintenance list so it is caught next time.
llmobs.why: After go-live, customers ask why an answer was wrong, why it was slow and why the bill went up, and you need evidence, not guesses. Security teams will also ask what customer data your logs contain. Almost every post-deployment FDE task, from debugging to cost cutting to proving value, starts with good traces and a feedback loop.

subtopics.title: What to trace in an LLM app
subtopics.body:
Observability means being able to answer new questions about a running system from the data it emits, without shipping new code. The Observability topic teaches logs, metrics and traces in general. LLM apps need extra fields, because the same code can behave very differently depending on the prompt and the model's reply.

A trace is the full record of one request. A span is one step inside it, with a name, a start time, a duration and attributes (key-value details). A typical support-agent trace has a root span for the whole run, and child spans for retrieval, each model call and each tool call.

For every model call, record: the model name and version, the prompt version (a label for the template, such as 'refund-v7'), the input and output token counts, the latency, the time to first token when streaming, the stop reason, and the computed cost. For tool calls, record the tool name, arguments, result size, errors and duration. For the run, record the user or session id, the tenant, the number of steps and the final outcome.

Whether to store full prompt and reply text is a decision, not a default. Full text makes debugging much easier, but it also copies customer data into another system. Many teams store full text with redaction for a short period, and only metadata after that.

Edge case: agents can loop. Record the step count on the root span and alert when it passes your turn cap, because a loop shows up as cost long before anyone complains.
subtopics.example: Fairholt Bank (made up) runs a mortgage FAQ assistant. Before tracing, the team only knew the monthly bill. After adding spans, one trace showed a question that took 11 seconds: 0.4 seconds of retrieval, two model calls of 1.5 seconds each, and a rate-lookup tool that took 7.6 seconds because it had no cache.

model, prompt version, tokens, latency, cost

subtopics.title: Spans for agents and OpenTelemetry GenAI
subtopics.body:
OpenTelemetry (OTel) is an open standard, with free SDKs in many languages, for producing traces, metrics and logs and sending them to any compatible backend. Using it means your traces are not locked into one vendor: you can switch backends by changing the exporter, the part that ships finished spans, usually over the OTLP protocol.

OTel publishes semantic conventions: agreed names for attributes so every tool reads them the same way. The GenAI conventions cover LLM work. Examples include gen_ai.operation.name (such as chat, execute_tool or invoke_agent), gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens and gen_ai.tool.name. These conventions are still marked as in development, and some names have changed between versions, so pin a version and check the current specification when you set it up.

For an agent, structure spans as a tree. The root span is the agent run. Under it, each loop iteration may have a model call span and one or more tool spans. If the agent calls a sub-agent, that sub-agent's run becomes a child span with its own children. The tree lets you answer 'which step was slow' and 'which step was expensive' at a glance.

Many libraries add spans for you. This is called auto-instrumentation: install a package and calls to a model SDK or a framework are traced without code changes. It is a fast start, but add your own spans for business steps, such as 'check eligibility', that no library knows about.

Edge case: spans carry context across services through a trace id in request headers. If one service drops the header, its spans start a new, disconnected trace.
subtopics.example: Fairholt's assistant calls a separate rate service. The FDE adds OTel to both, so the rate service's spans appear under the assistant's tool span in one tree. The code shows the same structure with an in-memory exporter, which prints spans instead of sending them.
subtopics.code:
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import SimpleSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export.in_memory_span_exporter import InMemorySpanExporter

exporter = InMemorySpanExporter()                 # in production: an OTLP exporter
provider = TracerProvider()
provider.add_span_processor(SimpleSpanProcessor(exporter))
trace.set_tracer_provider(provider)
tracer = trace.get_tracer("claims-agent")

with tracer.start_as_current_span("invoke_agent claims-helper") as root:
    root.set_attribute("gen_ai.operation.name", "invoke_agent")
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("chat MODEL") as llm:
        llm.set_attribute("gen_ai.operation.name", "chat")
        llm.set_attribute("gen_ai.request.model", "MODEL")
        llm.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.input_tokens", 1840)
        llm.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.output_tokens", 212)
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("execute_tool lookup_policy") as tool:
        tool.set_attribute("gen_ai.operation.name", "execute_tool")
        tool.set_attribute("gen_ai.tool.name", "lookup_policy")

for s in exporter.get_finished_spans():
    parent = s.parent.span_id if s.parent else None
    print(s.name, "| child" if parent else "| root", "|", dict(s.attributes))
# Output:
# chat MODEL | child | {'gen_ai.operation.name': 'chat', 'gen_ai.request.model': 'MODEL', 'gen_ai.usage.input_tokens': 1840, 'gen_ai.usage.output_tokens': 212}
# execute_tool lookup_policy | child | {'gen_ai.operation.name': 'execute_tool', 'gen_ai.tool.name': 'lookup_policy'}
# invoke_agent claims-helper | root | {'gen_ai.operation.name': 'invoke_agent'}

subtopics.title: Tools: Langfuse, LangSmith, Phoenix and cloud options
subtopics.body:
You rarely build a tracing backend yourself. Several tools specialise in LLM traces: they show span trees with prompts and replies, track cost, collect feedback, manage datasets and run evaluations on traces.

Langfuse is open source and can be self-hosted or used as a cloud service. It accepts OpenTelemetry data and has SDKs for Python and JavaScript. LangSmith is the commercial platform from the LangChain company; it works with or without LangChain, and self-hosting is offered on enterprise plans. Arize Phoenix is an open-source tool built on OpenTelemetry through the OpenInference conventions, often run locally during development. Cloud and monitoring vendors also have options, for example LLM monitoring features in general observability platforms such as Datadog, and tracing built into the major cloud AI platforms. Features and licences change often, so check each vendor's current documentation.

For an FDE the choice is mostly driven by the customer, not by taste. The key questions: may trace data leave the customer's network, which cloud and region, what the customer already uses for monitoring, who will operate the tool after you leave, and the cost at their traffic volume.

A practical pattern: instrument with OpenTelemetry, send to whatever the customer approves, and keep the option to switch. In a strict environment, self-host an open-source backend inside the customer's cloud account. In a lighter one, a managed service gets you started in an hour.

Edge case: some customers already have a central observability platform with an approved security review. Adding a second tool may take months of approval, so sending GenAI spans to the existing platform can be the fastest path.
subtopics.example: Fairholt Bank's security team says no customer text may leave their cloud region. The FDE self-hosts an open-source tracing backend in the bank's own account, with a 30-day retention setting, and sends metadata-only spans (no prompt text) to the bank's existing monitoring platform for alerts.

subtopics.title: Logging safely: redaction and retention
subtopics.body:
Traces are often the most sensitive data in an AI project. A single prompt can contain a customer's name, address, account number and complaint. If traces are copied into a third-party tool and kept forever, you have created a new store of personal data that nobody reviewed.

PII means personally identifiable information: data that identifies a person, such as a name, an email, a phone number or an ID number. Redaction means replacing PII with a placeholder, such as [EMAIL], before the data is stored. Pseudonymisation replaces it with a consistent token, such as user_4f2a, so you can still group one person's traces without knowing who they are.

Where to redact: in the application, before the exporter, so raw PII never leaves the process. Simple patterns (regular expressions) catch structured data like emails, phone numbers and card numbers. Names and addresses need named-entity recognition (NER), a model that finds names in text; open-source tools such as Microsoft Presidio combine both. No redactor is perfect, so combine it with access control and short retention.

Retention is how long data is kept. Set it deliberately, for example full text for 14 days to debug recent issues, and metadata (tokens, latency, cost, outcome) for 13 months for trends. Write it into the design doc so the customer's privacy officer can approve it. The Compliance topic explains the legal basis for these rules.

Edge case: redaction can break debugging when the bug is in the PII itself, such as a date format. Keep a small, access-controlled path to view raw data for approved incidents, and log each use.
subtopics.example: At Fairholt, a test found 312 email addresses and 41 card-like numbers in one day of traces. After adding redaction before export, a re-scan of the next day found zero of either, and the retention setting was fixed at 14 days for text and 13 months for metrics.

import re

PATTERNS = [
    ("EMAIL", re.compile(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+")),
    ("CARD",  re.compile(r"\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,16}\b")),        # 13 to 16 digits
    ("PHONE", re.compile(r"\+\d{1,3}(?:[ -]?\d{2,4}){2,4}\b")),  # international format
]

def redact(text):
    for label, pattern in PATTERNS:
        text = pattern.sub(f"[{label}]", text)
    return text

prompt = ("Hi, I'm Dana, dana.moss@example.com, card 4111 1111 1111 1111, "
          "call me on +44 7700 900 123 about my mortgage.")
print(redact(prompt))
# Output:
# Hi, I'm Dana, [EMAIL], card [CARD], call me on [PHONE] about my mortgage.

subtopics.title: Capturing user feedback as eval cases
subtopics.body:
User feedback is the cheapest signal of quality you will get. It comes in two forms. Explicit feedback is something the user does on purpose: a thumbs up or down, a star rating, a comment. Implicit feedback is inferred from behaviour: the user copied the answer, edited the draft heavily, asked the same question again, or escalated to a human.

Feedback is only useful if you can see what caused it. So the app should return the trace id with every answer, and the front end should send it back with the click. Then each thumbs down points to the full trace: the prompt, the retrieved documents, the tool calls and the reply.

The loop has four steps. Collect feedback with the trace id. Review negative feedback regularly, for example 30 traces a week, and label the root cause (retrieval miss, wrong instruction, tool error, model mistake, or 'user wanted something out of scope'). Fix the most common cause. Add each confirmed failure to the eval set, the fixed set of test cases from the Evals topic, with the correct expected answer, so the next release is tested against it.

Expect feedback to be sparse and biased: often only 1 to 5 percent of answers get a click, and unhappy users click more. Treat the rate as a trend, not a quality score, and do not optimise the prompt to the few loudest users.

Edge case: a thumbs down on a correct answer ('the policy says no refund') is still useful. Label it 'correct but unwelcome' so it does not become a wrong test case.
subtopics.example: Over two weeks, Fairholt's assistant got 180 thumbs down out of 9,000 answers. Review of 60 of them found 26 retrieval misses on a new product, 14 outdated rate answers, 12 correct-but-unwelcome and 8 other. The team re-indexed the product pages and added 40 new eval cases.
checklist: Every answer returns a trace id to the front end
Thumbs and comments are stored with the trace id
Negative feedback is reviewed on a fixed schedule
Each reviewed trace gets a root-cause label
Confirmed failures become eval cases with expected answers
Correct-but-unwelcome answers are labelled, not 'fixed'

import json

feedback = [
    {"trace": "t-101", "thumb": "down", "question": "Rate for the Green Home loan?", "label": "retrieval_miss",
     "expected": "Mention the 3.9% fixed rate from the Green Home page"},
    {"trace": "t-102", "thumb": "down", "question": "Can I skip a payment?", "label": "correct_but_unwelcome"},
    {"trace": "t-103", "thumb": "up",   "question": "What is an ERC?"},
    {"trace": "t-104", "thumb": "down", "question": "Overpay limit?", "label": "outdated_answer",
     "expected": "Say 10% per year, per the 2026 terms"},
]

new_cases = [
    {"id": f"fb-{f['trace']}", "input": f["question"], "expected": f["expected"], "source": f["trace"]}
    for f in feedback
    if f["thumb"] == "down" and f.get("label") not in (None, "correct_but_unwelcome")
]
with open("eval_cases.jsonl", "a") as out:              # append to the eval set
    for case in new_cases:
        out.write(json.dumps(case) + "\n")
print(len(new_cases), "new eval cases:", [c["id"] for c in new_cases])

subtopics.title: Online evals, sampling and dashboards
subtopics.body:
Offline evals run on a fixed test set before a release. Online evals run on real production traffic after it, because real users ask things your test set never imagined. Both matter; the Evals topic covers offline evals, and this is the production side.

You cannot afford to judge every trace with an LLM judge, so you sample. Sampling means evaluating a fraction, such as 5 percent, chosen fairly. A good trick is to hash the trace id and keep traces whose hash falls in the lowest 5 percent: the choice is random-looking but repeatable. Also evaluate 100 percent of the traces you care most about, such as those with thumbs down, errors or high cost.

What to score online: cheap code checks on every trace (valid JSON, answer length, a required citation present, no PII in the output), and sampled LLM-judge scores for things like groundedness (is the answer supported by the retrieved documents?) and helpfulness. Calibrate the judge against human labels first, as the Evals topic explains.

A quality dashboard shows these per day and per slice (customer, product, language, prompt version): volume, p50 and p95 latency, cost per conversation, error rate, thumbs-down rate and judge scores. Set alerts on sharp changes, for example groundedness dropping 10 points day over day, which often means a data or model change.

Edge case: a small slice can hide in an average. If French questions are 4 percent of traffic and fail badly, the overall score barely moves. Always check slices.
subtopics.example: Fairholt samples 5 percent of about 3,000 daily conversations, roughly 150, for a groundedness judge, and judges every thumbs-down trace. When a new prompt version shipped, the dashboard showed groundedness fall from 0.91 to 0.78 for the 'remortgage' slice only, and the team rolled it back the same afternoon.

import hashlib, random

def in_sample(trace_id, rate=0.05):
    h = int(hashlib.sha256(trace_id.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)
    return (h % 10_000) < rate * 10_000          # same trace id, same decision every time

random.seed(7)
traces = [{"id": f"t-{i}", "grounded": random.random() > 0.1,
           "slice": random.choice(["remortgage", "new loan", "fees"])} for i in range(3000)]

sampled = [t for t in traces if in_sample(t["id"])]
print("sampled", len(sampled), "of", len(traces))
for s in ["remortgage", "new loan", "fees"]:
    part = [t for t in sampled if t["slice"] == s]
    print(f"{s:<11} n={len(part):>3}  grounded={sum(t['grounded'] for t in part) / len(part):.2f}")
# Output:
# sampled 154 of 3000
# remortgage  n= 49  grounded=0.92
# new loan    n= 67  grounded=0.94
# fees        n= 38  grounded=0.84

labeling.plain: Data labeling means attaching the correct answer to examples, such as tagging each support ticket with its topic, so a model can learn from them or be tested against them. Human review means people checking the model's work, especially the cases it is unsure about. Doing this well needs clear written rules called guidelines, a way to measure whether two people agree, an expert to settle disagreements, and hidden test questions to keep quality steady. In production, a review queue sends risky or low-confidence items to people and saves their decisions as new labels.
labeling.analogy: It is like marking exam papers for a whole school. Teachers need a shared marking scheme with sample answers, a second marker checks a sample to see if they agree, a head of department settles disputed marks, and a few pre-marked papers are slipped into each pile to check that nobody's marking has drifted.
labeling.why: Almost every AI project an FDE runs needs labels: a golden set to prove accuracy to the customer, training data for a classifier, or reviewed outputs to catch errors after launch. Customers often assume their existing data is correctly labeled, and it rarely is. Knowing how to run a small, measurable labeling process is what turns 'the model seems good' into a number the customer trusts.

subtopics.title: Writing labeling guidelines with edge cases
subtopics.body:
A label is the answer attached to an item: 'refund request' on a support ticket, 'invoice total = 412.50' on a document, 'grounded' on a model reply. Labeling (also called annotation) is the work of adding those answers, and the people doing it are annotators. Labels are used two ways: as training data a model learns from, and as a golden set, the trusted answers your evals compare against (see the Evals topic).

The guideline is the document that tells annotators exactly how to label. It is the most important part of any labeling project, because most disagreements come from unclear rules, not careless people. A good guideline has:

1. The goal in one sentence, so annotators know what the labels are for.
2. The label list, each with a definition, two clear examples and one counter-example.
3. A decision order for items that seem to fit two labels, for example 'if money is requested back, choose refund, even if delivery is also mentioned'.
4. Edge cases: empty items, other languages, spam, items that fit no label. Always include an 'unclear' or 'other' option so people do not force a guess.
5. A version number and a change log.

Write the first draft with the customer's domain expert, then test it: label 30 items yourself, note every moment you hesitated, and turn each hesitation into a rule. Expect three or four versions before it settles.

Edge case: if the guideline changes, labels made under the old version may now be wrong. Store the guideline version with every label so you can find and re-check them.
subtopics.example: Orlwyn Home Goods (made up), an online furniture shop, wants tickets sorted into refund, delivery, account and other. In the pilot, 'my sofa arrived broken, I want my money back' was labeled delivery by one person and refund by another. Guideline v2 added the rule: any request for money back is refund, whatever the cause.

rows: The customer asks for money back
They only ask about a delay
Late, lost or damaged item, no money asked
It fits a label but is long
You cannot decide after the rules
You have not read the rules

checklist: Goal of the labels in one sentence
Every label defined with 2 examples and 1 counter-example
A decision order for overlapping labels
An 'other' and an 'unclear' option
Edge cases: empty, spam, other language
Version number and change log
Tested by labeling 30 items yourself

subtopics.title: Tools: Label Studio and spreadsheets
subtopics.body:
You need somewhere for annotators to see an item and record a label. There are three common choices, and the right one depends on volume, data type and the customer's security rules.

A spreadsheet is fine for a first batch of a few hundred text items. Put one item per row with columns for the item id, the text, the label (a dropdown built with data validation, so people cannot type 'Refund ' with a stray space), a notes column and the annotator's name. Its weaknesses: two people can see each other's answers, it cannot show images or PDFs well, and it is easy to sort one column and scramble the rows.

Label Studio is an open-source labeling tool you run with Docker or pip. You define the interface in a small XML config, import items as JSON or CSV, assign tasks to annotators, and export results as JSON or CSV. It supports text, images, audio, PDFs and model pre-labels, which are the model's guesses shown for a person to confirm or fix. Because you can host it inside the customer's network, it often passes security review where a cloud service would not. Hosted platforms and managed labeling vendors exist too, for large volumes or when the customer has no annotators.

Whatever the tool, check four things: each annotator can be shown items without seeing others' labels; every label is stored with who made it, when, and which guideline version; the export keeps the item id; and access follows the customer's data rules.

Edge case: pre-labels speed people up but also bias them toward the model's answer. Measure agreement without pre-labels at least once.

subtopics.title: Measuring agreement: percent and kappa
subtopics.body:
Inter-annotator agreement tells you whether your labels mean something. If two trained people, following the same guideline, cannot agree on an item, a model will not learn a stable answer for it either, and an eval built on those labels will be noisy.

To measure it, have two annotators label the same sample (50 to 200 items is typical) without seeing each other's answers. Then compute:

1. Percent agreement: the share of items where both chose the same label. Easy to explain, but it flatters you when one label is very common, because people agree on that label often by chance.
2. Cohen's kappa: (observed agreement minus chance agreement) divided by (1 minus chance agreement). Chance agreement is worked out from how often each person used each label. Kappa is 1 for perfect agreement, 0 for no better than luck, and can go below 0.

There is no official pass mark, but many teams read kappa below about 0.4 as weak, 0.4 to 0.6 as moderate, 0.6 to 0.8 as substantial and above 0.8 as strong. Treat these as rough guides. For three or more annotators, Fleiss' kappa or Krippendorff's alpha do the same job.

The number tells you whether there is a problem; the list of disagreements tells you what it is. Read every disagreement, group them, and look for a missing or unclear rule.

Edge case: if one label is extremely rare, kappa can be low even when agreement looks near perfect. Report percent agreement, kappa and per-label counts together.
subtopics.example: Two Orlwyn annotators, Ana and Ben, labeled the same 20 tickets. They matched on 16 (80 percent). Chance agreement from their label mix was 0.30, so kappa was 0.71, substantial. Two of the four disagreements involved 'other', which led to a clearer rule for it.
subtopics.code:
from collections import Counter

ana = ["refund","refund","delivery","refund","account","delivery","other","refund","account","delivery",
       "refund","delivery","account","refund","other","delivery","refund","account","delivery","refund"]
ben = ["refund","delivery","delivery","refund","account","delivery","refund","refund","account","delivery",
       "refund","delivery","other","refund","other","account","refund","account","delivery","refund"]

n = len(ana)
p_o = sum(a == b for a, b in zip(ana, ben)) / n          # observed agreement

ca, cb = Counter(ana), Counter(ben)
labels = set(ana) | set(ben)
p_e = sum((ca[l] / n) * (cb[l] / n) for l in labels)     # agreement expected by chance

kappa = (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e)
print(f"percent agreement {p_o:.0%}")
print(f"chance agreement  {p_e:.2f}")
print(f"Cohen's kappa     {kappa:.2f}")
for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(ana, ben), 1):
    if a != b:
        print(f"item {i:>2}: Ana={a:<8} Ben={b}")
# Output:
# percent agreement 80%
# chance agreement  0.30
# Cohen's kappa     0.71
# item  2: Ana=refund   Ben=delivery
# item  7: Ana=other    Ben=refund
# item 13: Ana=account  Ben=other
# item 16: Ana=delivery Ben=account

subtopics.title: Adjudication and gold questions
subtopics.body:
Adjudication means settling disagreements. An adjudicator, usually a senior annotator or the customer's domain expert, looks at every item where annotators disagreed and chooses the final label. The adjudicator also asks why the disagreement happened. If the guideline did not cover the case, they add a rule and a worked example, and the guideline version goes up. This loop is how guidelines become precise.

Some teams use majority vote instead: three annotators label each item and the most common label wins. It is cheaper than an expert for easy items, but a majority can still be wrong on hard ones, so hard or high-value items should still go to an expert.

Once items are settled, the trusted ones become gold labels. Gold questions are gold items mixed secretly into annotators' normal work, perhaps 5 to 10 percent of each batch. Because you already know the right answer, you can score each annotator continuously. Accuracy that drops over time is called drift: people get tired, forget a rule, or start a habit. Catching it early means retraining one person instead of relabeling a thousand items.

Steps: 1) pick 30 to 50 gold items that cover every label and the known edge cases; 2) mix them randomly into batches; 3) score each annotator weekly; 4) review anyone below a threshold with them, using the items they missed; 5) retire gold items people have seen too often and add fresh ones.

Edge case: if a gold item is itself wrong, you will punish good annotators. When several strong annotators all 'miss' the same gold item, re-check the gold label.
subtopics.example: Orlwyn hid 5 gold tickets in every batch of 50. After three weeks, one annotator's gold accuracy fell from 95 to 70 percent. The misses were all 'address change' tickets labeled delivery. A 10-minute review with the guideline example fixed it, and only her last two batches were re-checked.

gold = {"t01": "refund", "t02": "delivery", "t03": "account", "t04": "other", "t05": "account"}

# each annotator's answers on the hidden gold items, per week
answers = {
    "Ana":  {1: ["refund", "delivery", "account", "other", "account"],
             3: ["refund", "delivery", "account", "other", "account"]},
    "Dara": {1: ["refund", "delivery", "account", "other", "account"],
             3: ["refund", "delivery", "delivery", "other", "delivery"]},
}
THRESHOLD = 0.8
for person, weeks in answers.items():
    for week, labels in weeks.items():
        correct = sum(l == g for l, g in zip(labels, gold.values()))
        acc = correct / len(gold)
        flag = "  <- review with guideline" if acc < THRESHOLD else ""
        print(f"{person:<5} week {week}: gold accuracy {acc:.0%}{flag}")
# Output:
# Ana   week 1: gold accuracy 100%
# Ana   week 3: gold accuracy 100%
# Dara  week 1: gold accuracy 100%
# Dara  week 3: gold accuracy 60%  <- review with guideline

subtopics.title: Active learning: label what the model doubts
subtopics.body:
Labeling costs money and expert time, so you want each label to teach the model as much as possible. Active learning is a loop that chooses which items to label next based on what the current model finds hard, instead of picking items at random.

The most common form is uncertainty sampling:

1. Train a first model on a small labeled set.
2. Run it on the large pool of unlabeled items and get a probability for each label.
3. Measure how unsure it is. Least confidence uses 1 minus the top probability. Margin uses the gap between the top two probabilities; a small gap means the model is torn between two labels. Entropy looks at the whole spread of probabilities.
4. Send the most uncertain items to annotators.
5. Add the new labels, retrain, and repeat until accuracy on a fixed test set stops improving.

Items the model is already sure about teach it little. Items near its decision boundary teach it most. In many projects this reaches the same accuracy with noticeably fewer labels than random picking, though the gain varies by task.

Two cautions. First, keep your evaluation set random and fixed; if you evaluate on uncertainty-picked items, your numbers will not reflect real traffic. Second, pure uncertainty sampling can keep choosing near-duplicates or junk (spam is often 'uncertain'), so mix in some random items and remove duplicates from each batch.

With LLMs, the same idea applies: use the model's own confidence, disagreement between two prompts, or a judge score to pick which outputs a human should label next.
subtopics.example: Orlwyn had 40,000 unlabeled tickets and budget for 1,000 more labels. Instead of a random 1,000, the FDE ran the first classifier on the pool and sent the tickets with the smallest margin, plus 20 percent random ones. The snippet shows the selection step on five tickets.
subtopics.code:
# model probabilities for 5 unlabeled tickets (refund, delivery, account, other)
pool = {
    "t101": [0.94, 0.03, 0.02, 0.01],
    "t102": [0.48, 0.45, 0.04, 0.03],   # torn between refund and delivery
    "t103": [0.10, 0.85, 0.03, 0.02],
    "t104": [0.30, 0.28, 0.25, 0.17],   # unsure about everything
    "t105": [0.05, 0.05, 0.88, 0.02],
}

def margin(p):
    top2 = sorted(p, reverse=True)[:2]
    return top2[0] - top2[1]              # small gap = unsure

ranked = sorted(pool, key=lambda t: margin(pool[t]))
for t in ranked:
    print(t, f"margin={margin(pool[t]):.2f}")
BUDGET = 2
print("send to annotators:", ranked[:BUDGET])
# Output:
# t104 margin=0.02
# t102 margin=0.03
# t103 margin=0.75
# t105 margin=0.83
# t101 margin=0.91
# send to annotators: ['t104', 't102']

subtopics.title: Human review queues in production
subtopics.body:
After launch, labeling does not stop; it moves into the product. A human review queue (also called human-in-the-loop review) is a list of items the system is not allowed to act on alone. A person checks each one, approves or corrects it, and the decision is saved as a new label.

What goes into the queue is a routing rule, agreed with the customer:

1. Low confidence: the model's confidence is below a threshold, such as 0.70.
2. High risk: the action is costly or hard to undo, such as a refund above 200 dollars or a medical or legal topic, whatever the confidence.
3. Random audit: a small share, such as 2 percent, of items the model handled alone, so you can measure its real accuracy on the traffic it is trusted with.

The threshold is a trade-off with people's time. A lower threshold sends fewer items to people but lets more mistakes through. Set it using a labeled sample: for each possible threshold, count how many items would be queued and what the error rate would be on the rest, then choose with the customer's operations lead, who knows how many reviewers they have.

Design the reviewer screen well: show the item, the model's suggestion and its reason, and make approve, correct and escalate one click each. Track queue size, waiting time and how often reviewers change the model's answer. That override rate is a live accuracy signal; if it climbs, something changed. Corrected items feed the eval set and the next training round, as the LLM observability topic describes for feedback.

Edge case: reviewers who approve almost everything may be rubber-stamping. Random audits and gold items in the queue catch this.
subtopics.example: Orlwyn now auto-routes about 78 percent of tickets. Tickets below 0.70 confidence, or asking for more than 200 dollars back, go to a queue of two agents. Their overrides, about 9 percent of queued items, become new labels each week.
subtopics.code:
THRESHOLD = 0.70
AUDIT_RATE = 0.02
import hashlib

def route(ticket):
    if ticket["refund_amount"] > 200:
        return "review: high risk"
    if ticket["confidence"] < THRESHOLD:
        return "review: low confidence"
    h = int(hashlib.sha256(ticket["id"].encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % 100
    if h < AUDIT_RATE * 100:
        return "auto + audit"              # repeatable random sample
    return "auto"

tickets = [
    {"id": "T-881", "label": "refund", "confidence": 0.93, "refund_amount": 45},
    {"id": "T-882", "label": "delivery", "confidence": 0.61, "refund_amount": 0},
    {"id": "T-883", "label": "refund", "confidence": 0.97, "refund_amount": 640},
    {"id": "T-884", "label": "account", "confidence": 0.88, "refund_amount": 0},
]
for t in tickets:
    print(t["id"], t["label"], t["confidence"], "->", route(t))
# Output:
# T-881 refund 0.93 -> auto
# T-882 delivery 0.61 -> review: low confidence
# T-883 refund 0.97 -> review: high risk
# T-884 account 0.88 -> auto

glossary: Label
The correct answer attached to an item, such as a category, a value or a yes/no judgement.
Annotator
A person who adds labels to items by following the guidelines.
Labeling guidelines
The written rules that define each label, with examples, counter-examples and edge cases.
Golden set
A set of items with trusted labels used to evaluate a system.
Inter-annotator agreement
How often different annotators give the same label to the same item.
Cohen's kappa
An agreement score for two annotators that corrects for agreement expected by chance.
Adjudication
Settling a disagreement between annotators by an expert who picks the final label.
Gold question
An item with a known answer hidden in normal work to check annotator accuracy.
Drift (annotator)
A gradual change in how a person labels, usually a slide away from the guidelines.
Active learning
Choosing which items to label next based on where the model is most unsure.
Pre-label
A model's suggested label shown to a person to confirm or correct.
Human-in-the-loop
A design where people review or approve some model decisions before they take effect.

voice.plain: A voice agent is an AI system that talks with people over the phone or another audio channel. It listens to the caller, turns speech into text or understands the audio directly, decides what to say or do with an LLM and tools, and speaks back. In production it has to connect to the phone network, stream audio in small pieces over a live connection, know when the caller has finished speaking, stop talking when interrupted, and reply fast enough to feel natural. It also has to follow rules about recording calls, handling card numbers and telling callers they are speaking with an AI.
voice.analogy: It is like a skilled receptionist working through a relay of interpreters: one writes down what the caller says, one decides the answer, one reads it aloud. Each hand-off takes time, so the relay only feels natural if everyone starts passing notes before the other has finished, and stops at once when the caller cuts in.
voice.why: Contact centers and customer-service companies are among the biggest buyers of AI agents, and many deployments are phone calls. An FDE on these projects connects the agent to the customer's phone system, tunes turn-taking and latency on real noisy calls, and works with legal on consent. Demos that feel great in a browser often fail on real phone lines, and that gap is exactly the FDE's job.

subtopics.title: The pipeline: cascade or speech-to-speech
subtopics.body:
The Multimodal topic introduced speech-to-text (STT), text-to-speech (TTS) and the idea of a voice latency budget. This topic is about running a voice agent on real phone calls, where each design choice shows up as cost, delay and risk.

There are two main designs.

1. The cascade: VAD, then streaming STT, then an LLM (with tools), then streaming TTS. Each part is a separate component you can choose, swap and test. You get a text transcript of both sides for free, which helps with logging, evals, guardrails and audits. The cost is delay: every hand-off adds time, and tone of voice is lost when speech becomes text.

2. Speech-to-speech (also called a realtime or native audio model): one model takes the caller's audio in and produces audio out. Several providers offer realtime APIs of this kind, usually over a WebSocket. It can respond faster, keep emotion and handle interruptions more naturally. You get less control at each step, fewer vendor choices, and the text you log may be a separate transcription.

A hybrid is common: a speech-to-speech model for the conversation, with a text transcript produced in parallel for logs, and tool calls for the actual actions.

How to choose: list the customer's must-haves (languages, regulated steps, tool calls, required voice), then test both designs on 20 to 50 real or realistic recorded calls. Compare turn latency, task success, cost per minute and how easy failures are to diagnose.

Edge case: accents, loud rooms and long account numbers stress both designs. Test them on purpose.
subtopics.example: Tarrowby Dental Group (made up) wants an after-hours line that books and moves appointments. Because every booking must call the practice system and be read back exactly, the FDE chose a cascade with text at every step, and planned to test a speech-to-speech option later for the general FAQ calls.

subtopics.title: Telephony: PSTN, SIP and number providers
subtopics.body:
Most voice agents answer ordinary phone calls, so you need to connect the old phone system to your code. Key terms:

1. PSTN (public switched telephone network): the worldwide phone network that ordinary phones use.
2. Phone number provider (a CPaaS, communications platform as a service): a company that rents you phone numbers and gives you an API to answer, place, transfer and record calls. You configure what happens when a call arrives, often by pointing the number at a webhook URL on your server.
3. SIP (Session Initiation Protocol): the standard protocol for setting up internet phone calls. A SIP trunk connects a company's phone system (PBX or contact-center platform) to the outside network. Enterprise customers often already have one, and want the agent connected to their existing numbers and call center instead of new numbers.
4. Media stream: the live audio of the call, which the provider forwards to your server, usually over a WebSocket.

The usual flow: a call arrives; the provider sends a webhook to your server; your server answers with instructions to open a media stream to a WebSocket address; audio flows both ways until someone hangs up or you transfer the call.

FDE work here is mostly integration with the customer's existing phone setup: which numbers route to the agent and when (after hours only?), how to transfer to a human queue with the conversation summary attached, what caller ID data arrives, and who owns the SIP configuration. Plan time for the customer's telecom team; changes often go through their change process.

Edge case: phone audio is usually 8 kHz and compressed with mu-law (G.711), much lower quality than a laptop microphone. Test with real phone calls, not a browser demo.
subtopics.example: Tarrowby's practices use a hosted contact-center platform. The FDE rented one test number from a provider first, then worked with Tarrowby's telecom partner to forward after-hours calls over the existing SIP trunk. The snippet shows the kind of instruction many providers accept when a call arrives: open a two-way audio stream to your WebSocket server.

subtopics.title: Streaming audio over WebSockets
subtopics.body:
A WebSocket is a connection that stays open so both sides can send messages at any time. That suits phone audio: the caller's voice arrives continuously, and your agent must send audio back while still listening. (The API styles topic compares WebSockets with ordinary request-response HTTP.)

Audio is sent in frames: small chunks, often 20 milliseconds each. Phone audio at 8,000 samples per second with 1 byte per sample (mu-law) is 160 bytes per 20 ms frame. Because WebSocket messages here are usually JSON text, the bytes are base64-encoded, which turns binary data into text and makes it about a third larger.

A typical session has message types: a start or connected message with call details, a stream of media messages with audio, marks or acknowledgements to know when your audio finished playing, a clear message to drop queued audio (used for barge-in), and a stop message when the call ends. Exact names differ by provider, so read their media stream docs.

Practical rules:

1. Never block the receive loop. Run STT, the LLM and TTS as separate async tasks so incoming frames keep flowing.
2. Match formats: if the phone sends 8 kHz mu-law and your STT expects 16 kHz PCM, convert (resample) in one place.
3. Send audio back in real time, not all at once, or you cannot stop it cleanly on barge-in.
4. Handle disconnects: log the call id, close STT and TTS sessions, and never leave a paid session running.

Edge case: a slow server that falls behind builds up a backlog; the agent then answers questions from seconds ago. Monitor the gap between frame timestamps and processing time.
subtopics.example: Tarrowby's server receives about 50 frames per second per call. At 40 simultaneous calls that is 2,000 messages per second, so the FDE ran one async task per call and load-tested with recorded audio before go-live. The code builds the frames for one second of audio.
subtopics.code:
import base64, json

SAMPLE_RATE = 8000          # phone audio: 8,000 samples per second
BYTES_PER_SAMPLE = 1        # mu-law uses 1 byte per sample
FRAME_MS = 20

frame_bytes = SAMPLE_RATE * BYTES_PER_SAMPLE * FRAME_MS // 1000
audio = bytes(range(256)) * 32                 # stand-in for 1 second of audio
audio = audio[:SAMPLE_RATE]

frames = [audio[i:i + frame_bytes] for i in range(0, len(audio), frame_bytes)]
msg = {"event": "media", "streamSid": "MZ-demo",
       "media": {"payload": base64.b64encode(frames[0]).decode()}}
text = json.dumps(msg)

print("bytes per frame:", frame_bytes)
print("frames per second:", len(frames))
print("base64 payload length:", len(msg["media"]["payload"]))
print("one JSON message:", len(text), "characters")
# Output:
# bytes per frame: 160
# frames per second: 50
# base64 payload length: 216
# one JSON message: 284 characters

subtopics.title: Turn-taking, barge-in and VAD
subtopics.body:
In a real conversation people take turns without thinking. A voice agent has to decide, many times a second, whether the caller is still talking. Getting this wrong is the most common reason voice agents feel rude or slow.

Voice activity detection (VAD) is a small, fast model or rule that labels each audio frame as speech or not speech. Endpointing (end-of-turn detection) uses VAD plus a silence timer: if there has been no speech for, say, 500 ms, the turn is over. Choosing that wait is a trade-off:

1. Too short and the agent cuts people off when they pause to think or read a number.
2. Too long and every turn feels slow, because the wait is added to all other delays.

Better systems adjust the wait: shorter after a complete sentence, longer after 'my number is...', or they use a turn-detection model that looks at the words as well as the silence.

Barge-in is when the caller speaks while the agent is talking. The agent should stop its audio within a few hundred milliseconds, clear any queued audio and listen. Then it must update the conversation history to record only the part of its reply the caller actually heard, or the LLM will assume the caller heard things they did not.

Edge cases: background TV or a second person triggers false barge-ins, so require a minimum speech length, such as 200 ms, before interrupting. Short sounds like 'mm-hm' while the agent talks are backchannels, not interruptions; many teams ignore very short speech during agent audio.

Test turn-taking with real callers reading long numbers and pausing mid-sentence.
subtopics.example: At Tarrowby, callers reading their 10-digit patient number were cut off after the fourth digit. Logs showed pauses of 600 to 700 ms between digit groups, longer than the 500 ms endpoint. The FDE raised the wait to 1,000 ms only when the agent had just asked for a number, and kept 500 ms elsewhere.
subtopics.code:
# 1 = speech, 0 = silence, one value per 20 ms frame
frames = [1]*25 + [0]*15 + [1]*20 + [0]*30        # talk, pause 300 ms, talk, silence
FRAME_MS = 20

def end_of_turn(frames, silence_ms):
    silent = 0
    for i, f in enumerate(frames):
        silent = 0 if f else silent + FRAME_MS
        if silent >= silence_ms and any(frames[:i]):
            return i * FRAME_MS                   # time the agent decides to reply
    return None

for wait in (200, 500):
    t = end_of_turn(frames, wait)
    print(f"wait {wait} ms -> turn ends at {t} ms")
# with 200 ms the agent jumps in during the caller's 300 ms pause

def is_barge_in(speech_ms, agent_speaking, min_ms=200):
    return agent_speaking and speech_ms >= min_ms  # ignore short 'mm-hm'

print("mm-hm (120 ms):", is_barge_in(120, True))
print("real interruption (450 ms):", is_barge_in(450, True))
# Output:
# wait 200 ms -> turn ends at 680 ms
# wait 500 ms -> turn ends at 1680 ms
# mm-hm (120 ms): False
# real interruption (450 ms): True

subtopics.title: The latency budget and how to cut it
subtopics.body:
Callers judge a voice agent mostly by how fast it replies. Latency here means the time from the caller's last word to the first sound of the agent's reply. Human conversation gaps are often a few hundred milliseconds, and many teams aim for roughly 800 ms to one second for an agent, with a strict limit on the slow tail (p95).

A latency budget splits that target across stages, so each owner has a number:

1. End-of-turn wait (endpointing silence).
2. STT final transcript after the turn ends.
3. LLM time to first token (TTFT), including any retrieval.
4. TTS time to first audio for the first sentence.
5. Network and telephony in both directions.

Tool calls add a sixth line whenever the agent must look something up.

Ways to cut it, roughly in order of payoff:

1. Stream everything and start TTS on the first sentence, never on the full reply.
2. Tune endpointing; each 100 ms saved here is saved on every turn.
3. Keep the prompt short and the reply short; long prompts raise TTFT (prompt caching can help, see the LLM cost topic).
4. Use a smaller, faster model for simple turns.
5. Host components in the same region as the telephony provider.
6. For slow tools, say a short filler such as 'Let me check that' while the tool runs, or fetch likely data (the caller's record) when the call starts.

Measure per stage in production, per turn, and look at p95, not only averages. One slow tool can ruin one call in ten while the average looks fine.

Edge case: fillers help once; repeated on every turn they sound robotic.
subtopics.example: Tarrowby's first build measured about 1,450 ms at p50. Stage logs showed a 700 ms endpoint wait and TTS started only after the full reply. Cutting the wait to 400 ms (with a longer wait kept for numbers) and streaming the first sentence to TTS brought p50 to about 950 ms, inside the budget below except on turns with a tool call. The code checks a per-turn log against the budget.
subtopics.code:
import statistics as st

budget = {"endpoint": 400, "stt_final": 100, "llm_ttft": 250, "tts_first": 120, "network": 80}
turns = [  # measured per turn, in ms
    {"endpoint": 410, "stt_final": 90, "llm_ttft": 240, "tts_first": 110, "network": 70},
    {"endpoint": 400, "stt_final": 110, "llm_ttft": 280, "tts_first": 120, "network": 90},
    {"endpoint": 420, "stt_final": 100, "llm_ttft": 910, "tts_first": 130, "network": 80},  # tool call
    {"endpoint": 390, "stt_final": 100, "llm_ttft": 230, "tts_first": 115, "network": 75},
]
print("budget total:", sum(budget.values()), "ms")
for stage, limit in budget.items():
    vals = [t[stage] for t in turns]
    worst = max(vals)
    flag = "  <- over budget" if worst > limit * 1.2 else ""
    print(f"{stage:<10} median {st.median(vals):>5.0f}  worst {worst:>4}  budget {limit}{flag}")
totals = [sum(t.values()) for t in turns]
print("turn totals:", totals)
# Output:
# budget total: 950 ms
# endpoint   median   405  worst  420  budget 400
# stt_final  median   100  worst  110  budget 100
# llm_ttft   median   260  worst  910  budget 250  <- over budget
# tts_first  median   118  worst  130  budget 120
# network    median    78  worst   90  budget 80
# turn totals: [920, 1000, 1640, 910]

subtopics.title: Testing, recording consent and compliance
subtopics.body:
Voice agents fail in ways a text chat never shows: noise, accents, people talking over the agent, bad lines. Testing needs three layers.

1. Component tests: STT accuracy on the customer's own recordings, especially names and numbers (the Multimodal topic covers word error rate), and TTS pronunciation of product names.
2. Scripted call tests: a set of scenarios (book, cancel, wrong number, angry caller, caller who switches language) run as simulated calls, where a second bot plays the caller with recorded or synthetic speech. Check task success, tool calls made and turn latency. Run them before every prompt or model change, like any eval set.
3. Live pilot: real calls on a small share of traffic, with a human listening to a sample daily and an easy transfer to staff.

Compliance questions to settle with the customer's legal team before launch:

1. Recording consent. Rules differ by place. Some US states require every party on a call to consent to recording, and many countries have similar rules. A clear message at the start of the call is the usual approach.
2. AI disclosure. Some laws and many company policies require telling callers they are speaking with an automated agent.
3. Payment cards. Card numbers must not end up in recordings or transcripts; pause recording, or send the caller to a dedicated secure payment step.
4. Retention and location of recordings and transcripts, under privacy law such as GDPR.
5. Outbound calling rules. Automated and AI-voiced outbound calls are regulated in many places; in the US the FCC has said AI-generated voices count as artificial voices under the TCPA.

Edge case: always provide a way to reach a person, and test that the transfer works after hours.
subtopics.example: Before Tarrowby's pilot, the FDE ran 120 scripted calls across 12 scenarios nightly. One scenario, a caller speaking over the greeting, failed 30 percent of the time until barge-in was fixed. Legal approved a greeting that discloses the AI and the recording in one sentence.
checklist: Greeting discloses the automated agent and recording
Consent rule checked for every region callers come from
Card numbers never reach recordings or transcripts
Retention period and storage region agreed in writing
Transfer to a person works, including after hours
Scripted call suite runs before every change
Daily human review of a sample of live calls

scenarios = [
    {"name": "book cleaning", "expect_tool": "book_slot", "got_tool": "book_slot", "p95_ms": 910},
    {"name": "cancel", "expect_tool": "cancel_slot", "got_tool": "cancel_slot", "p95_ms": 870},
    {"name": "talks over greeting", "expect_tool": "book_slot", "got_tool": None, "p95_ms": 1400},
    {"name": "wants a person", "expect_tool": "transfer", "got_tool": "transfer", "p95_ms": 640},
]
LATENCY_LIMIT = 1000
passed = 0
for s in scenarios:
    ok = s["got_tool"] == s["expect_tool"] and s["p95_ms"] <= LATENCY_LIMIT
    passed += ok
    print(f"{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}  {s['name']:<20} tool={s['got_tool']}  p95={s['p95_ms']} ms")
print(f"{passed}/{len(scenarios)} scenarios passed")
# Output:
# PASS  book cleaning        tool=book_slot  p95=910 ms
# PASS  cancel               tool=cancel_slot  p95=870 ms
# FAIL  talks over greeting  tool=None  p95=1400 ms
# PASS  wants a person       tool=transfer  p95=640 ms
# 3/4 scenarios passed

glossary: Voice agent
An AI system that holds spoken conversations, often over phone calls, and can take actions with tools.
Cascade
A voice design that chains speech-to-text, an LLM and text-to-speech as separate components.
Speech-to-speech model
A model that takes audio in and produces audio out directly, without a separate text step.
PSTN
The public switched telephone network, the worldwide network used by ordinary phones.
SIP
Session Initiation Protocol, the standard for setting up internet phone calls; a SIP trunk links a phone system to the outside network.
WebSocket
A long-lived two-way connection where both sides can send messages at any time.
Frame
A small chunk of audio, often 20 milliseconds, sent as one message.
Mu-law (G.711)
A common phone audio encoding at 8 kHz using 1 byte per sample.
VAD
Voice activity detection: deciding whether a frame of audio contains speech.
Endpointing
Deciding that the caller has finished their turn, usually after a stretch of silence.
Barge-in
The caller speaking while the agent is talking, which should make the agent stop and listen.
Time to first token (TTFT)
How long an LLM takes to return the first piece of its reply.
practice: Draw the cascade for a pizza-ordering line and write a latency budget with a number for each stage that adds up to 900 ms.
Run the end-of-turn code with your own frame pattern: a caller reading a 10-digit number in groups with 600 ms pauses. Find the smallest wait that does not cut them off.
Write 10 scripted call scenarios for a dental booking line, each with the expected tool call, including three hard ones (noise, interruption, switching language).
Draft the first sentence a caller hears that discloses the AI and the recording in under 20 words, and list which facts you would check with legal.
Stretch: rent a trial number from a telephony provider, connect it to a small WebSocket server that logs frame counts per second, and call it from your phone.
